item.research_question: How do mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering affect the phase evolution, microstructure refinement, and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys?
item.material_system: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions of Cobalt, Chromium, Iron, Nickel, and Titanium)
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying using a planetary ball mill (QM-1SP4) at 400 rpm for 1–6 hours under argon atmosphere, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) in a vacuum at 900–1000 °C for 10 minutes with a heating rate of 50 °C/min
item.test_conditions: Vickers hardness testing at 0.05 kN load with 15 s dwell time; compressive strength tests at a displacement rate of 0.5 mm/min (strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹); XRD analysis with Cu-Kα radiation (2θ range 20°–80°); SEM and TEM for microstructural analysis
key_findings: The milled powder exhibited a nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% FCC and 17% BCC phases.
The bulk alloy achieved a Vickers hardness of 675 Hv, surpassing commercial alloys like Stellite (500 Hv).
The material demonstrated a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa at a sintering temperature of 1000 °C.
The Avrami exponent (n) for the FCC phase was 2.09, while for the BCC phase it was 1.48, indicating interface-controlled growth mechanisms.
The FCC phase nucleation predominantly occurred after 5 hours of milling, whereas BCC nucleation and growth occurred simultaneously from the start.
The reaction rate constant (k) for the FCC phase was 0.0305/min, and for the BCC phase it was 0.0412/min.
Density increased from 6.57 g/cm³ at 950 °C to 6.98 g/cm³ at 1050 °C, approaching the theoretical density.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the exceptional hardness and strength to the synergistic effects of mechanical alloying and SPS, which refine the microstructure, increase dislocation density, and promote a dual-phase (FCC/BCC) solid solution structure. The high titanium content induces lattice expansion, and the refined grain size contributes to solid solution strengthening. The kinetic analysis suggests the phase formation follows a nucleation and growth mechanism governed by interface-controlled growth.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the casting process suffers from porosity and non-uniformity, and that the CoCrFeNiTi alloy in its standard form suffers from relatively low hardness and strength prior to this specific processing.
item.future_work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors, but mentions that the kinetics of alloys have not been thoroughly examined in numerous prior investigations and that the mechanical properties of the CoCrFeNiTi alloy have remained largely unexplored.
quotes: The milled powder exhibited nanocrystalline solid solution microstructure with grain sizes below 48 nm, composed of 83% face–centered cubic (FCC) and 17% body–centered cubic (BCC) phases.

Mechanically, the bulk CoCrFeNiTi alloy exhibited exceptional strength attributes, as evidenced by a Vickers hardness value reaching 675 Hv, along with a compressive strength of 1894 MPa and a yield stress of 1238 MPa.
The Avrami exponent (n) indicates that the formation kinetics of the CuCrFeTiNi high–entropy alloy (HEA) are primarily governed by interface–controlled growth mechanisms.
